etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English idiote, ydiote, from Old French idiote (later idiot), from Latin idiota, from Ancient Greek ἰδιώτης (idiṓtēs, “a private citizen, one who has no professional knowledge, layman”), from ἴδιος (ídios, “one's own, pertaining to oneself, private”). Doublet of idiota.

definitions.definition: (derogatory) A person of low general intelligence.
(derogatory) A person who makes stupid decisions; a fool.

(obsolete, medicine, psychology) A person of the lowest intellectual standing, a person who lacks the capacity to develop beyond the mental age of a normal four-year-old; a person with an IQ below 30.

quote.citation: 1896, Clifton Johnson, “Folks”, in What They Say in New England (non-fiction), Boston, Massachusetts, United States: Lee and Shepard Publishers, page 105:
quote.text: Idiots were thought to be peculiarly under the care of the Deity, and it was believed that those who treated them kindly would be blessed.

quote.citation: 1956, Parliament of the United Kingdom, “Part I, section 7”, in Sexual Offences Act 1956‎[1], page 2:
quote.text: It is an offence for a man to have unlawful sexual intercourse with a woman whom he knows to be an idiot or imbecile.
